why: It dates a souvenir trade at a temple gate to the early modern period and names its mechanism: at Kumano and elsewhere the shugenja became half-monk and half-layman and came to sell souvenir goods, and later, as demand expanded, specialist souvenir shops came into being and formed a gate town - the goods being talismans and amulets above all, with lucky dolls, toys, picture books and sacred medicines beside them - the custom spreading from the middle of the early modern period as the highways were made up and commoner pilgrimage spread through the pilgrimage guides and oshi. That is the souvenir row our gate quarters draw, on a dated statement rather than on inference. Its limits are that it dates the flourishing to mid-Edo, so an earlier gate carries fewer such shops; and that it speaks of Japan, while this setting's temple economy also draws on China.

It puts the sweet trade where the record can support it. Once the Edo period came in and traffic on the highways increased, the sweets sold at the teahouses along the way developed in their own directions out of what travelers said of them, and travelers spreading word of those sweets was the greatest occasion for confectionery developing in the provinces. Its limits are that it places the teahouse on the HIGHWAY rather than at a temple gate, so it supports sweets on the pilgrim road and not a sweet-seller at the gate; and that it is a general statement about the period with no one place or date attached.

It fixes the direction of a flow this record had backwards: in old times believers donated incense sticks, candles, lamp oil and gold paper to temples and monasteries for use in the offerings, and later gradually gave money in their place, which is why the money itself is named for the two goods. So incense and lamp oil reach a Chinese temple as a DONATION rather than leaving it as stock - the same relation the Japanese omamori already gave us, and the reason no third-party religious-goods shop is drawn at a temple's own gate. Its limits are that it is a stub of a few hundred characters carrying no references at all, the weakest work this page cites; that the conclusion drawn from it, no third-party shop at the gate, rests on the page's SILENCE rather than on anything it says; that it gives no temple's accounts and no annual figure, so the size of that income is still unsourced; and that it describes the practice generally rather than in a dated period.

It is the only readable text found that draws the comparison our gate rule rests on - the European barbican's narrow neck preventing a sortie against the wengcheng as a protected staging ground roomy enough to pass a body of troops either way. It is careful and consistent with the manuals it illustrates, but a claim resting on it alone is one specialist's synthesis rather than an attested statement, and it describes China, not Japan.

It gives real numbers, from the body responsible for the monument, for the two features our city gates draw and had none for - a barbican court and a canal gate - and it settles the barbican's PLAN, which is roughly square rather than urn-shaped. Its limits are that it describes one exceptional surviving gate of a great Jiangnan city rather than a norm, and that its figures are of the monument as it stands after restoration.

It is the closest thing the East Asian record offers to a sally port's FUNCTION - a small concealed opening kept shut and opened when needed - which is the term our postern comparison leans on hardest. Its limits are that it describes Japanese castles rather than a Chinese city wall; and that the better sources for it, a cultural-property survey or the city that holds the famous surviving example, were not reached.

Four measured clear widths at one Ming gate are exactly what a rule about the opening a road passes through needs, and they are the only such set this record could read. Its limits are that this is the grandest gate of a Ming capital rather than a provincial seat's, so it stands at the top of the band and not in the middle of it; and that the figures describe the monument as restored.

The record says the century of that inherited corner is disputed, and this is the readable page carrying the side of the dispute the encyclopedia article does not: a Tang origin against a Yuan one. Its limits are severe and are why it is used only for that: it reports what it says the field accepts without citing a study, and it concerns one corner of one wall.

It is a primary text that states a dimension AND the reason for it - the bed is kept small because water cannot otherwise be spread evenly over it by hand, and because nobody should have to step into it - which is the rarest and most useful shape of evidence a drawing rule can rest on, and it sizes the very thing this record was asking about, a garden serving a walled town. Its limits are that it is Northern Wei north China, far earlier than the Ming and Edo anchor; that the text is read from a crowd-transcribed wiki copy rather than a critical edition, so a disputed character would have to be settled against a scholarly one; and that its measures are in bu and mu, which this record has not converted from a metrology source - and a Northern Wei bu is not a Ming bu, so converting with a later metrology would be positively wrong rather than merely unsupported. Every figure in feet derived from it is our own arithmetic.

The gate suburb is a shape our city maps draw at every main gate, and this is the only readable page found that describes one as a place with trades and a count rather than defining the word. Its limits are that this is the busiest gate of a capital and one trade's premises, so the count is a ceiling for a provincial seat rather than a measurement of one; and that the figure carries no date beyond "at its height".

It is the one readable case of a gate suburb that formed for the OPPOSITE reason to the general pattern this record quotes - the walled ground filled first and the overflow went outside - which is worth a reader knowing beside the pattern. Its limits are that one case is not a refutation of a general pattern, and that this is a frontier garrison on the Mongolian trade route rather than an ordinary county seat.

Our setting makes a merchant's walled and gated compound a granted right rather than a purchase, and this is the historical arrangement it is modeled on, stated by three independent works in the language of permission and tied to rank and to office. Its limits are that they describe Tokugawa Japan while the walls on our city maps take their form from the Chinese side of the setting's ancestry; and that they regulate the GATE and say nothing about a compound wall.

It carries both halves this record needs from one page - the privilege as a lord's grant tied to office and to merit, which is the setting's own arrangement almost word for word, and the later practice that contradicts the setting's rule that money cannot buy it, which is what lets the deviation be stated precisely rather than assumed. Its limits are that they describe Tokugawa Japan only; and that none of them says a wall or a gate could be obtained this way, so the departure is recorded for the surname privilege and read across to the compound by us.

It names the back-to-back pair our rows are packed in - mune-wari, one roof over two ranks sharing a rear wall - as the standard form rather than as a deduction, and gives the unit its size. Its limits are that its subject is Edo, so the dimensions are the standard nine-shaku-two-ken formula rather than a measured survey; and that it describes the rented tenement and not the merchant house in front of it.

It gives the depth rule from the other end - what a plot's frontage buys is one row along the lane or two facing rows, never a third rank behind them - which is the historical reason our rows stack at most two deep, and it puts the single entrance where the map puts it. Its limits are that it describes the Japanese town house of Kyoto and Edo rather than the Chinese courtyard housing the setting also draws on; and that the frontage figures are typical rather than surveyed.

It gives the measured width our drawn lane is judged against, and the widening at the shared well that the map draws, both for exactly the kind of lane the map is packing. Its limits are that the width is a range for Edo back-lane tenements rather than a survey figure, and that the article covers the modern sense of the word alongside the historical one.

It dates the institution our record says had lapsed before the period these cities are modeled on, which is what disposes of the dusk-curfew explanation for lodging outside a gate. Its limits are that its own footnotes into the Song urban-history literature would be the better citation; and that a single date for a change that came unevenly across a large empire is a simplification.

It answers whether a place below the capital kept an organized fire watch, which our fire-tower rule turned on, and it does so with a named primary source for the Ming case and a dated edict for the Qing one. Its limits are that the Ming detail reaches us through the article's paraphrase of the Wanshu zaji rather than from the text itself, and that it establishes a WATCH and not a standing lookout tower.

It supplies the tower-to-neighborhood ratio our dispersal rule rests on, from two works that state it separately, and it separates what was per-machi (the watch house) from what was not (the tower). Its limits are that the ratio is Edo's, the largest wooden city there was, in one era, so a provincial seat two orders of magnitude smaller is being reasoned to rather than described; and that the Japanese arrangement is only half of the setting's ancestry.

It is the source that puts the bell, the ladder and the gear at the TOWN's watch post, which is where our unwalled-seat fire posture places them and which no page had previously supported. Its limits are that it is specific to Edo-period Japanese towns, and that it attaches all of it to the neighborhood watch house and nothing at all to an intendant's office, which is the half of our posture that stays unsupported.

It attests the stored water our fire posture lists, dated to the period and to the town. Its limits are that it is a short article, Japanese and Edo-specific, giving no count of how many a street kept and no size, so nothing on the map is drawn from it.

It turns "fireproof kura" from an adjective into something a map can draw and a reader can check, and it names the rice store as one of the kinds such a building was built for, which is the thing our unwalled seat protects first. Its limits are that it is Japanese, and that its fire-survival claim is stated generally rather than from a study, so it supports the form and not a survival rate.

It identifies the building our fire posture says was protected before anything else, and confirms that the tax rice had a store of its own rather than sitting in a general warehouse. Its limits are that it describes the village store rather than one inside an intendant's compound, which is the attachment this record still cannot support; and that it gives no dimension.

It makes the identification our unwalled tax seat rests on a published one rather than this record's own guess, and it names the rice store inside the compound, which is the thing the fire posture says was fireproofed. Its limits are that it describes Tokugawa Japan only, so the Chinese county seat our maps also draw on is not covered by it.

It gives the documented order of magnitude for the draft animals a settlement on a trunk road had to hold standing, which is what our gate caravan cluster is sized against, from the ministry that maintains the road. Its limits are that it states an OBLIGATION on a station and not the animals of any one arriving train; and that it is the Japanese post system rather than a Chinese wagon route, which is the other half of the setting's ancestry.

It is the evidence that a trunk-road settlement swamped by arriving traffic did not answer with a bigger yard but by widening the ring it drew animals from, which is what withdraws this record's town-against-city contrast. Its limits are that they describe a corvee obligation rather than commercial stabling; and that the system is Tokugawa Japanese.

It gives the density our temple-quarter rule needs - several small shrines to one town block - and the reason a block would raise one, which is a placement fact a map can use. Its limits are that it describes one cult; that its statement about material runs against the vermilion wooden shed the map draws, which the record now labels a drawing convention on that evidence; and that it says nothing about a temple quarter, so the placement between temples remains unsupported.

It supplies the count a capital's amenity ratio is built from, given twice by two independent works, which is what turns a per-head figure from an assertion into arithmetic a reader can follow. Its limits are that a guild roll counts members rather than premises; and that the page gives no population, so the one-per-so-many ratio this record quotes is our own division against a figure taken from elsewhere.

It counts the domains that survived to the 1871 edict, 261, which is the nearest readable count to the end of the Edo period. The sentence giving 261 carries no footnote (the article is flagged for lacking inline citations; Jansen, The Making of Modern Japan, which it lists, is the closer source that would trace the count). The count is taken just after the period rather than in it, once some domains had already been dissolved, so it likely understates the late-Edo figure: the same article's account of 1869 implies about 262 to 276 domains, and other pages give other figures (274 daimyo in 1869, "just under 300" domains). It is a round order of magnitude, not an exact census.

It sets modern paddies, each fed from a supply canal and emptied into a drain, against the old-style irrigation the village keeps, in which water passes from paddy to paddy, and says the old way saves water. It describes one hill village as it survives today; it does not say how common the form was, nor count the village's ditches, and the same village keeps many weirs. It presents the form as suited to this village in particular, which has long suffered from water shortage and whose cold water warms as it passes through the paddies, so it is weak evidence that the form was the general pre-modern practice; and it dates the weirs' place-names to Muromachi documents but gives no date for the paddy-to-paddy form itself, calling it only old-style. Updated 2022.

The physics is the same in any age and country: a smooth surface such as open water drags on the wind less than land does, so the wind near it stays stronger. Its figures are for the sea, large open water and ice, not for a sheet of small ponds divided by planted dikes, so it supports the direction of the effect over the ponds, not how strong the wind is at any one dike. The sentence cited rests on its own reference, Lubosny's Wind Turbine Operation in Electric Power Systems (2003), p. 17, and the standard textbook for the smooth-against-rough point is Oke's Boundary Layer Climates (1987), p. 54; neither was read here.

It is the one page read that gives how thickly the dike mulberry of the Pearl River delta was planted and how it was trained, and it describes the system the map's dike-pond hamlet is drawn from. It dates the system's history (fruit-dike ponds before the ninth century, mulberry dikes after the sixteenth) but gives its planting figure only as the practice "to this day" (至今, translated), with no date; that the figure describes the twentieth-century system is this project's inference. So its planting density is evidence for the later form of the system, not a measured pre-modern figure, and its mu is presumably the modern one of about 667 square meters, not the Qing mu; it names no crown width. A peer-reviewed study of the same delta system, Zhong Gongfu's 1980 paper in Acta Geographica Sinica, was not read here and may give a better figure.

It is the page read that turns the paces of a sixth-century treatise into meters, and it gives the two reckonings of the pace side by side. Its table has a Wei-Sui row (220-266 and 581-618) and nothing for the centuries between, so a foot for the 540s is carried across a gap the table leaves - and probably carried short: zh.wikipedia's own table (中国度量衡, itself unsourced by dynasty) gives the northern foot of the Qimin yaoshu's time as about 29.6 cm against this row's 25.5 cm, which would make feet reckoned from the row some 14% small. It gives the pace at five and at six feet without saying which held when. Its mu (614.4 square meters) and qing are from a separate table of the units promulgated in 1915, a Republican standard built on a 32 cm foot, not any dynasty's measure: a Northern Song area in mu put through them comes out about 8% larger than one reckoned from the article's own Song row (240 square paces of 1.54 m, about 569 square meters). The Ming row is itself a range (0.3008-0.3190 m). Its length table rests on a single citation, Schinz's The Magic Square (1996), a book on the planning of ancient Chinese cities rather than a study of measures, and the article itself notes that it omits the several kinds of foot in use in some periods.

It is the page read for Suzhou as a premodern Chinese city laid over an engineered water network, the example given of a city whose water ran into canals rather than marsh. Its description of the canals is general and undated beyond "as late as the early 20th century", and that sentence is itself taken from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, a late-Qing observation made before most of the city's industry. It says nothing of drainage at all: it describes the canals as linking the city's islands to the countryside, never as where the city's water or the fields' water went, so "a city draining into engineered water" is our reading of the network rather than the page's statement, and the fields' drainage rests on no page read.

It is one of the few readable accounts of the garden of a jin'ya, the kind of walled office-residence our compounds draw, and it says the garden was a pond garden seen from the shoin. Its limits are that the jin'ya was dismantled after the domains were abolished and what stands there now is a park opened in 1985, the shoin moved back in the Shōwa era, the page not saying to its old place, and the garden made then from the drawing, which the page does not reproduce, so that the site itself files the garden as Shōwa work, its Kyoto-style planting of Kitayama cedar is the restorers' choice, and the page does not say whether the two tiers, the upper one reaching toward a restaurant built with the park, are the drawing's or the restorers'; and that it was the seat of a domain, grander than a county post, and is one example rather than a pattern.

It counts the kinds of garden kept at one group of rural samurai houses: of seven, one pond garden and six dry landscapes. Its limits are that Chiran was a Satsuma settlement of rural samurai, a regional form whose gardens the page itself links to those of Ryukyu; that the seven are the gardens that survived to be designated, not a count of all the houses, and they lean to the settlement's leading households (three are Sata houses, a family of the old lords' line that held Chiran's highest offices), so the count describes its better houses more than its ordinary ones; and that it dates only the street layout, to about 280 years ago, not each garden.

It gives, in standard reference works, the lantern's parts, its named kinds, and that it entered tea gardens and ordinary gardens from the Momoyama period. Its limits are that the single lantern at the center front of a shrine or temple is the Britannica entry's in a sentence, and is what the lantern was originally (本来は) - the arrangement it came with, with Buddhism, from China and Korea, its oldest survivor of the early Nara period - not a statement of later or Edo-period practice, which the page does not give; and that nothing on it speaks of a residence's court.

We use it for the word and for Ise's rings as the great-shrine case. Its limits: flagged by Wikipedia since August 2017 as lacking sources and possibly containing original research (last edited December 2022), so its history of the form (brushwood first, stone later) is unsourced; its one worked example is the imperial shrine; it does not say what an ordinary village shrine had.

A standard encyclopedia names practice against a standing timber as the school's basic technique and dates its founder. Its limits are that it is an excerpt of a few lines from an older edition, and gives no size, count or setting for the post. It also describes the practice as one Satsuma school's own: the entry calls the conservatively surviving regional character of Jigen-ryū singular (特異), so it does not show that striking posts were a general feature of training grounds elsewhere, and a map that draws them at a generic training ground extends the source rather than following it.

It says the practice ground is open-air and practice is barefoot and mostly tategi-uchi, which is the setting a practice ground in the open needs. Its limits are that it is a practitioners' page, and that the school is Nodachi Jigen-ryū, which the page says is a different school from Jigen-ryū (示現流); and that an open-air, barefoot ground for tategi-uchi is one Satsuma school's own practice, so it supports an open practice ground and not the form of a roofed training hall elsewhere in Japan.
It supports the order wood-then-stone. Its limits: no dates or sources for the change, so it gives the order and no chronology.

A signed entry in a modern encyclopedia (Saitō Shin'ichi, in Nipponica) says the three long arrest weapons were kept on hand at checkpoints and guard posts. It also says an early Edo screen painting shows them stood in a row, and from that it guesses they were used early on as symbols of order and dignity. Its limits are that it says only that the weapons were kept on hand at guard posts, not that they were stood up or how they were stored there; that "symbol of order" is the author's guess ("であろう") from one painting, not a stated fact; that it describes arrest weapons, not practice weapons; that its one picture of them standing is a theater's entrance on a screen painting, not a guard post; and that it gives no rack, size or count.
It is a plain witness that an ordinary shrine with an arch and no fence was unremarkable. Its limits: one unnamed shrine, and the absence is incidental to the question; it is not a survey.

It gives China's village temple as a single hall of about 100 to 400 m². Its limits: no date for its figures, which describe present-day Fujian temples, many rebuilt, and may be building areas rather than compounds.
It separates the old rite from the newer pavilion. Its limits: silent on whether small shrines had the pavilion or only a basin.

It is a scholar-written reference account of the veranda of the warrior household's shoin-style house, which is the house our residences draw. Its limits are that Hirai's examples of the inner veranda are all great houses (the Nijō castle palace, the Katsura villa, a temple guest hall), while the older Heibonsha entry on the same page says the houses of middle and lower warriors had almost no corridors before the end of the Edo period, so the inner irikawa bears on a great residence more than a lesser one; that it describes the Japanese house only, a form the entries call peculiar to Japan; that it gives the width of the floor boards but not of the veranda itself, and that its dating of the farmhouse veranda is hedged by the entry's own "though it differed by region".

It gives a width for the veranda-corridor our residences draw and the social line across which corridors and wrap-around verandas were and were not built. Its limits are that a dictionary width is a norm and not a survey (one surviving house, Katsura, has a half-ken irikawa); that the dictionary's one-ken definition is undated and its only example of that sense is from a Meiji magazine (Fuzoku Gaho, 1902), so the page does not by itself tie the one-ken width to the Edo period; and that the corridor excerpt is cut short on the page and names no author.

It is a scholar-written account of how a great warrior house was divided and ringed, the model our residences scale down. Its limits are that it describes the largest establishments of the early seventeenth century, not a provincial posting.
It attests the offered sumo and its ring at ordinary shrines. Its limits: no date for the village practice and no size for a village ring.
It fixes what the word means on our residence plans. It says nothing of which houses had one or how long it ran.

It defines the feature. Its limits: a stub flagged as unsourced; its formal classes come from the Meiji-to-war shrine-ranking system, and it says it is unknown whether the word was used before modern times; its examples are all great shrines, and it says nothing of how often a village shrine had one.
unsettled: The feature is defined across eras while its formal classes are Meiji-to-war, which the cut-off table does not cleanly place.

why: It is the best-described surviving case of shoin halls set in echelon and grown by accretion, and it gives veranda widths, in ken, for the Ko-shoin, the Naka-shoin and the Gakki-no-ma (none for the Shin-goten). Its limits are that this is a princely villa with sukiya elements, not a warrior's official residence; that its ken is the long side of a tatami mat as the article defines it, about 2 meters by the article's own figures (7.5 ken = 15.8 m), not the six-shaku ken; that the Naka-shoin's tatami veranda was at first an open veranda, enclosed later (probably when the Shin-goten was added), so it shows the hall as altered, not as first built; and that its dates are scholars' estimates from the princes' diaries and the 1976-1982 restoration's findings, the Shin-goten's date and purpose disputed.

It attests the covering house over a small sanctuary. Its limits: flagged as unsourced and as possible original research, and its covering-house sentence has no citation; no prevalence and no date for the form at village shrines (its one pictured example, Ujigami Shrine's c. 1060 sanctuary under its covering house, is a great shrine).
